title: Islamophobia 'as bad as the 1980s' says murdered boy's sister

input.evidence_text: Islamophobia 'as bad as the 1980s' says murdered boy's sister - BBC News Image source, Family Image caption, Ahmed Iqbal Ullah's death inspired renewed efforts to tackle Islamophobia and racism across Greater Manchester By Elle McDade North West Published 43 minutes ago The sister of a 13-year-old boy who was murdered by a fellow pupil in their school playground 40 years ago has said Islamophobia "is as bad as it was in the 1980s". Ahmed Iqbal Ullah, a British Bangladeshi, was stabbed at Burnage High School in Manchester on 17 September 1986. A subsequent inquiry into the teenager's death examining racism and violence in Manchester's schools concluded that race was a key factor in the Bangladeshi's murder. Speaking on the 40th anniversary of Ahmed's loss, Selina Ullah said: "I've got children and grandchildren now and for them to experience what I experienced - what my generation, my friends, my brother experienced - is heartbreaking and terrifying." Image source, Family Image caption, Selina Ullah says social media can fuel racism His killer, 13-year-old Darren Coulburn, was jailed for life with a minimum of 21 years. Two days before the murder, Ahmed had intervened when Coulburn attacked a younger Asian pupil in Ladybarn Park, near his school. The following day, Ahmed and Coulburn had a physical altercation in the park. The next morning, Coulburn brought a knife to school and stabbed Ahmed in the stomach. Four decades on from her brother's murder, Ullah said she would like to see the perpetrators of daily acts of racism to be held accountable. She said she wanted laws such as the Race Relations Act to be properly implemented. The Act was first introduced in 1968, as the second of three laws related to race in the United Kingdom. input.evidence_text: A £600,000 fund set up after the deadly attack on Heaton Park Synagogue has sparked criticism after none of the money was given directly to Jewish organisations The funding was awarded to Salford City Council as part of a government recovery programme following the attack during Yom Kippur last year, in which Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby were killed Council leaders said the money would support projects tackling antisemitism, racism and division, but local community leaders have questioned how it has been distributed A council spokesperson said the authority stood "in solidarity" with the Jewish community and had provided support to Jewish organisations and communities The funding forms part of a £2m package from the Home Office intended to support long-term recovery following the October attack According to the Local Democracy Reporting Service , external , a council report approved on 22 September said the money would be used for projects that "challenge direct and indirect antisemitic and racist rhetoric" and improve community cohesion

input.summary: The garden, built by specialist craftspeople from China and the UK, opens to visitors on Saturday
input.evidence_text: The centrepiece of what the RHS describes as Europe's largest and most authentic classical Chinese garden will open to visitors in Greater Manchester on Saturday after more than eight years in the making The Yangzhou Scholars' Garden at RHS Garden Bridgewater in Salford is the result of a collaboration between organisations in China, the RHS and Greater Manchester's Chinese community Specialist craftspeople from China used traditional techniques "rarely seen outside China" to create the garden, the RHS said Marcus Chilton-Jones, head of RHS Garden Bridgewater, described it as a "lasting symbol of friendship, cultural exchange and shared learning." title: Man denies charges over Manchester synagogue attack

input.lead: Hekmat Ali Hakim, 49, of Salford, denied failing to disclose information to the police
input.summary: Hekmat Ali Hakim, 49, of Salford, denied failing to disclose information to the police
input.evidence_text: Man denies charges over Manchester synagogue attack - BBC News Image source, PA Media Image caption, Hekmat Ali Hakim, 49, of Salford, denied failing to disclose information relating to the Manchester synagogue attack. Published 25 September 2026 An alleged "close associate" of the Manchester synagogue knife attacker has denied failing to disclose information in relation to the terror attack. Worshippers Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby were killed when Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, drove into the gates of the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue in October last year, and then began attacking with a knife, wearing a fake suicide belt. Hekmat Ali Hakim, 49, of Salford, Greater Manchester, appeared via video link from prison at the Old Bailey on Friday and pleaded not guilty to failing to disclose information. Prosecutor Jonathan Polnay KC said the Iraqi national was a "close associate of Jihad Al-Shamie, who carried out a terrorist attack at a synagogue in Manchester". He said Hakim allegedly "failed to disclose that information". The charges state that between 13 August and 3 October last year, Hakim had information which he knew or believed might be of material assistance in preventing the commission by Al-Shamie of an act of terrorism in the UK. They also state he failed to disclose that information as soon as reasonably practicable to a police officer. A trial date was set for 17 May 2027 at Manchester Crown Court. Hakim was formally arraigned on Friday. The defendant, who was accompanied by an interpreter throughout the hearing, was remanded in custody. Al-Shamie, a Syrian-born British citizen, was shot dead by police on the day of the attack, which took place on Yom Kippur - the holiest day of the year for Jews. She ended up becoming their head of accounts, and held sole responsibility for all the financial aspects of the company, Minshull Street Crown Court heard in February this year However, from 2008, she abused her position to steal from them in three 'discreet' ways; by claiming unauthorised overtime payments, stealing petty cash and unauthorised use of the company's credit card The total loss to the company was £128,352, the court heard. The fraud was revealed in June 2019 when it was discovered Clarke had been using the credit card. title: Northern Roots opens: A major new green space for Oldham welcomes first visitors

input.lead: An exciting new visitor attraction has opened its doors in the heart of Oldham
input.summary: An exciting new visitor attraction has opened its doors in the heart of Oldham
input.evidence_text: An exciting new visitor attraction has opened its doors in the heart of Oldham. The first phase of Northern Roots is now open, marking an exciting chapter at the home of what will be the UK’s largest urban farm. Delivered through a partnership between the Northern Roots charity and Oldham Council, the new 160-acre development gives people the chance to enjoy nature closer to home, improving local health and wellbeing, supporting education, creating local jobs, and playing an important role in Oldham's ongoing regeneration. The project is transforming 160-acres of underused land next to Alexandra Park into a landmark destination, and the opening day gave visitors their first opportunity to experience the Welcome Building, cafe, Forestry Skills Centre, Urban Farm, and an expanding network of trails, orchards, woodland and wetlands. Thousands of visitors from across Oldham and beyond flocked to the site to experience Oldham’s newest major visitor attraction. Families enjoyed an outdoor play area with a sandpit, climbing frames and water play, and free activities including face painting, outdoor games, live music, a bubble performer, unicyclist and roaming stilt walkers. title: Council secures court order following unauthorised encampment at Oldham Edge

input.lead: Oldham Council has secured a court order requiring the removal of an unauthorised encampment from Oldham Edge
input.summary: Oldham Council has secured a court order requiring the removal of an unauthorised encampment from Oldham Edge
input.evidence_text: Oldham Council has secured a court order requiring the removal of an unauthorised encampment from Oldham Edge. Council officers first visited the site on Thursday 6th August following concerns from residents and people using the park. Officers spoke to those at the encampment, who said they intended to leave by Saturday 8th August. As the site had not been vacated, the Council returned with support from Greater Manchester Police on Tuesday 11th August. A formal direction was served under Section 77 of the Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994, requiring those at the encampment to leave and remove their vehicles and belongings. The Council also provided information about authorised sites in Greater Manchester, along with advice about health, wellbeing and reporting hate crime. After the direction was not followed, the Council began court proceedings. On Monday 17th August, Tameside Magistrates’ Court granted an order requiring the removal of the encampment. The site was vacated later that day. A significant amount of waste was left behind, which has now been removed by the Council’s cleansing team. A Council spokesperson said: “We understand the concerns raised by residents and people using Oldham Edge, and we thank them for their patience while we followed the legal process. “We always try to resolve unauthorised encampments through discussion and voluntary cooperation wherever possible. However, when the site was not vacated as agreed, it became necessary to take further action. “We worked closely with Greater Manchester Police throughout to make sure the situation was handled lawfully and proportionately. “The encampment has now left and our cleansing team has completed the clean-up, allowing the area to be returned to the local community.”

title: Is the funding market getting harder and what could that mean for Manchester? | Manchester Digital

input.lead: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing.
input.summary: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised
input.evidence_text: Tech investment isn't slowing down, but the pattern of investment is changing. As investors grow increasingly selective, the capital ecosystem has become polarised. More capital is being concentrated in fewer companies while the market for exits remains difficult Financial news recently added another dimension to that discussion. AI-related shares fell last week after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for a slower approach to the development of increasingly capable AI models. Nvidia finished the day down 3.4%, SoftBank fell 10.7% in Tokyo Additionally, the Bank of England is predicted to increase interest rates later this year, which could affect the North West's tech funding landscape by raising the cost of capital across the board, compressing valuations, pushing investors toward profitability over growth-at-all The British Business Bank's 2026 Small Business Equity Tracker found that equity investment into UK smaller businesses fell 4% to £12.3bn in 2025. Seed deal numbers fell 27% and venture deals fell 13%. AI companies attracted 44% of all investment into smaller businesses while the Beauhurst recorded £14.4bn of UK equity investment across 2,799 deals in the first half of 2026 but three AI companies accounted for 29% of all the capital raised. Those very large rounds can make the overall market look stronger than it feels to businesses raising at seed or Ser Beauhurst's analysis shows that UK equity investment more than doubled between 2017 and 2021 to £32.2bn while annual exits remained at around 400 to 500. An exit takes a median of four years from a funding round

input.evidence_text: As AI adoption gathers pace, organisations are under growing pressure to invest and demonstrate where the technology can deliver meaningful business value This lunchtime session brings together senior technology leaders with first-hand experience of putting AI into practice. Drawing on real-world examples and lessons from delivery, the panel will explore what it takes to move from ambition and experimentation to measurable results The discussion will offer a candid view of the decisions, foundations and trade-offs involved. Speakers will share what they have learned from implementing AI, including the technical, operational and organisational challenges encountered along the way There will also be an opportunity to put your questions to the panel and connect with fellow technology leaders over lunch 📅 Date: Thursday 1st October 2026 🕒 Time: 12pm-2pm 📍 Location: No.1 Circle Square 💷 Price: Manchester Digital members - Free (4 x tickets per company) Non members - £30 Spaces are limited - secure your place to gain insight from these senior leaders and connect with peers
